analysis.one_liner: Bans new federal leases for coal, oil, and gas on public lands and offshore waters.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Natural Resources Committee and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Keep It in the Ground Act of 2016 would have stopped the federal government from selling new leases to companies that extract coal, oil, and natural gas from public lands and offshore waters, including the Gulf of Mexico and the Arctic, Atlantic, and Pacific Oceans. The bill stated it was federal policy to keep public fossil fuels in the ground to avoid the most dangerous impacts of climate change, with narrow exceptions for imminent national security threats and for pre-existing lease contracts that would be materially breached. It was introduced by Rep. Jared Huffman with 24 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially communities exposed to climate change impacts and residents of coastal and Gulf regions near offshore drilling, would gain from ending the expansion of federal fossil fuel extraction. Future generations would be the largest beneficiaries, since leases sold now allow extraction for decades.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would end new federal leasing of coal, oil, and natural gas, including offshore leases in the Arctic, Atlantic, and Pacific Oceans and the Gulf of Mexico, which are areas where new leases commit the United States to decades of additional fossil fuel extraction.

The bill declared it the policy of the United States to keep federal fossil fuels in the ground for the benefit of the people of the United States, in order to avoid the most dangerous impacts of climate change.

The bill included exceptions for imminent national security threats and for pre-existing nonproducing lease contracts that would be materially breached, so it would not have immediately revoked existing contracted rights.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies that profit from federal leases would bear the main cost, losing access to new public lands and waters. Workers and communities in coal- and oil-dependent regions, along with state and federal treasuries that collect royalty revenue from federal leases, would bear costs from a faster transition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel companies and extraction regions

drawbacks.text: Ending new federal leases would cut off royalty revenue that federal and state governments collect from energy companies extracting on public lands and waters, money that funds treasuries and programs, and some supporters acknowledged the transition cost for coal- and oil-dependent communities and workers.

Critics of lease bans argue that restricting US supply can raise energy prices and shift production to countries with weaker environmental rules rather than reducing total consumption. The bill's own text concedes the disruption by carving out exceptions for pre-existing contracts that would be materially breached.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The climate benefit of not selling new leases is long-term and diffuse, while the costs — lost royalty revenue and disruption for extraction-dependent workers and communities — are near-term and concentrated. The bill provided exceptions to protect existing contracts, but it did not include transition funding for affected workers or revenue replacement for states, so the honest weighing depends heavily on how much one values avoided future emissions versus near-term economic disruption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the bill on February 11, 2016, the same day it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
Five days later, on February 16, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action appears in the record.
The bill had 24 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican cosponsors.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill died without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies that hold or sought federal leases on public lands and offshore waters, since no restriction was ever enacted and federal leasing continued unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 24 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 24 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: Rep. Rob Bishop
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the record shows no action after the subcommittee referral.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to end federal fossil fuel leasing, which would cut off access to public lands and offshore waters.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 supporters (the sponsor plus 24 cosponsors) were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never reached a floor vote, so there were no roll calls.

industries.note: The bill would ban new offshore leases in the Gulf of Mexico and the Arctic, Atlantic, and Pacific Oceans and end new federal leasing generally. Oil and gas companies profit directly from these leases, so the industry's interest in the bill ran against the climate benefit the bill offered the public.

The bill would end new federal coal leases and bar renewal or extension of nonproducing federal coal leases except under narrow contract-breach exceptions. Coal companies rely on federal leases for a large share of US production.
Restricting new fossil fuel supply would, over time, favor renewable energy producers competing for the same electricity and fuel markets.
